newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss sweep finds only small Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss sweep finds only small Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Funds owned by Jewish victims of the Holocaust made up only a tiny part of the unclaimed wealth Swiss banks have found so far as they pore over claims for dormant accounts on their books, an official said on Tuesday.

"It was around 11,000 Swiss francs ($8,750)," banking ombudsman Hanspeter Haeni told reporters when asked how much Jews had held of the 1.6 million Swiss francs ($1.3 million) in dormant accounts covered by claims submitted recently and judged valid.

Haeni was presenting his first progress report on a search launched at the start of the year, when Swiss banks under pressure from world Jewish groups empowered his office with coordinating queries from heirs of Holocaust victims.
His brief covered any accounts declared dormant, meaning banks had heard nothing from the owners for 10 years.
Haeni said he would continue his search but warned he did not expect to find the huge wealth in Holocaust accounts that has been speculated about by Jewish critics and media reports.
"I do not expect any spectacular results," he said.

Haeni said he believed many accounts had already been found in a previous 1960s sweep of Swiss bank vaults and that some accounts still left might yield nothing. He gave the example of one he discovered with now-worthless 1930s Romanian bonds.

Haeni said 892 detailed questionnaires filled out by people who believed they had claims to a dormant account had yielded 11 accounts at Swiss banks. He did not name the successful applicants or the banks involved.
"Around 70 percent of the applications were from relatives of victims of the Nazi regime," he told a packed news conference.
Judging from their names or information from applicants, Jews held five of the 11 dormant accounts found so far, he said.
Three of them were Jews murdered in Hitler's drive to exterminate European Jewry, he said. Two others were Jews who lived in Romania and were dispossessed by anti-Semitic laws.
In the other six cases, it was unclear if the orignial owner was a Jew or else it was obvious from the dates of activity that that account became dormant before or long after the Holocaust.
It was unclear from his remarks how much of the 1.6 million francs covered by valid claims had already been reported.

The Swiss Bankers Association said in February that 38.7 million francs ($30.7 million) had been found in dormant accounts of all kinds, not just those opened by Jews hoping to hide their assets from the Nazis in secretive Swiss banks.

Haeni, whose work has been dismissed by Jewish critics as a "cruel hoax" designed simply to protect Swiss banks, said his office would continue to act as the central contact point for Holocaust account inquiries for an indefinite period.

Haeni said he had contacted his critics at the World Jewish Congress (WJC) last week to ask for their cooperation but was discouraged when the charge of cruel hoax was repeated on Monday in remarks by a WJC vice president.
"Let us hope there is an official answer from the WJC to my query that does not reply with defamation," he said.
Haeni said up to 20 detailed inquiries were still coming in daily and that he would make another public appearance in mid-1997 to give an update on the status of the hunt.
Swiss banks deny accusations by Jewish groups and plaintiffs in two class-action suits that they may be sitting on billions of dollars in unclaimed wealth left behind by Hitler's victims.

To probe charges of a cover-up, major Jewish groups and Swiss banks agreed in May to set up an independent panel headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul Volcker to search for any wealth that escaped two previous sweeps by banks.
Haeni said it was up the Volcker commission to judge whether the banks were acting in good faith, but added: "I have the impression that the banks are working very well."
The commission will also work with a historical panel due to win parliament's approval next month with a broad mandate to probe Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
